title: Noetherian generic freeness for finite algebra-module pairs
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian integral domain [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], let $B$ be a commutative $R$-algebra of finite type, meaning $B\cong R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/J$ for some finite $n\geq0$ and an ideal $J$, and let $M$ be a finitely generated $B$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. There exists $0\ne a\in R$ such that $M_a$ is a free $R_a$-module. Here $R_a=R[1/a]$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away], and $M_a$ is the localized module [def-weil-pbc-module-localization-away] of fractions $m/a^j$, with $m/a^j=m'/a^k$ if and only if $a^u(a^km-a^jm')=0$ for some $u\geq0$. Free means isomorphic to $\bigoplus_{i\in I}R_a$ for some set $I$, not necessarily finite.

proof.text: We use the following elementary fraction calculations throughout. Localization preserves a short exact sequence: a fraction mapping to zero has a numerator whose image is killed by a power of the localization element; multiplying its numerator and denominator by that power puts the numerator in the original kernel, where it lifts from the first term. Injectivity follows by the same zero-fraction criterion, and surjectivity follows by lifting a numerator. Localizing twice, first at f and then at b/f^j, is the same as localizing at fb: both f and b become units, and the fraction maps in the two directions are inverse. The same statements hold for modules and for localization at all nonzero scalars.

If a module is free with basis (e_i), its localization has basis (e_i/1): a finite sum of fractions has a common denominator, and a relation becomes a relation in the original module after multiplying by a further localization power. A short exact sequence with free quotient splits by choosing a lift of each quotient basis vector and extending linearly; the union of a basis of the kernel and those lifts is a basis of the middle module. These observations allow further localization and extensions of free modules, including infinite-rank modules.

Put K=Frac(R) and B_K=(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}B. This is a finite type K-algebra: localize a finite polynomial presentation coefficientwise. If B_K is nonzero, field Noether normalization supplies an injective finite map K[T_1,...,T_e] into B_K, and the dimension theorem identifies e with dim(B_K), hence this dimension is a finite nonnegative integer. Prove the assertion by strong induction on this integer, simultaneously for all Noetherian domains R and all finite type algebra-module pairs. Before the induction, handle B_K=0: the equality 1/1=0 gives a nonzero a in R annihilating 1 in B; then B_a=M_a=0, free with empty basis. At induction level d, first prove the assertion for domain algebras S with dim(S_K)=d, using the induction hypothesis only for pairs of smaller generic dimension. Afterwards step 8 recovers all pairs of dimension d.

For the domain algebra S at level d, a nonzero element f of the kernel of R to S makes S_f=0. Otherwise R embeds in S. Apply Noether normalization over a domain: it gives an injective polynomial subalgebra P=R[y_1,...,y_e], an intermediate algebra S\prime finite as a P-module, and nonzero f with S\prime_f=S_f. Replace the base by R_f and S by S_f. The base remains a Noetherian domain: an ideal of R_f is generated by the images of generators of its contraction to R, and R_f embeds in K. We now have an inclusion P=R_f[y_1,...,y_e] into S_f finite as a P-module. Localizing at all nonzero base elements preserves injectivity by the fraction criterion and finiteness by localizing the finite module generators. Applying the dimension theorem to K[y_1,...,y_e] into S_K gives e=d. At the end, any further nonzero scalar b/f^j is replaced by the nonzero original scalar fb, as in step 1. Thus it suffices to work with a finite domain extension P=R[y_1,...,y_d] contained in S.

proof.text: Let F=Frac(P). Localizing S at P\setminus\{0\} gives a finite-dimensional F-vector space E generated by the images of finitely many P-module generators of S. Choose a maximal linearly independent subfamily z_1,...,z_r from those images; it is a basis since any omitted generator is dependent on it. Take each z_i in S by using the original generators. A P-linear relation among the z_i is an F-linear relation, so all coefficients vanish, and S embeds in E since S is a domain and P embeds in S. Therefore the map P^{\oplus r} to S sending the standard basis to the z_i is injective. Put N=S/\sum_i Pz_i; its images of the finitely many module generators of S generate N over P. Express each such generator in the F-basis z_i and multiply all finitely many nonzero denominators in these coordinates. Their product g is a nonzero polynomial in P and sends every generator into \sum_i Pz_i; hence gN=0. Thus N is finite over the finite type R-algebra C=P/(g). This gives the short exact sequence 0 to P^{\oplus r} to S to N to 0, with no unproved support assertion.

proof.text: The coefficient inclusion R into K sends g to a nonzero g_K in K[y_1,...,y_d]. Coefficientwise localization and quotient identify C_K with K[y_1,...,y_d]/(g_K). The dimension theorem applied to the identity map on K[y_1,...,y_d] gives dimension d. A prime chain of length t in its quotient lifts by inverse image to a strict chain of primes containing g_K; its first prime is nonzero, so prepending the zero prime of the polynomial domain gives a chain of length t+1. Consequently dim(C_K)<d if C_K is nonzero, and C_K=0 is the already handled zero case. In particular for d=0, g_K is a nonzero constant and C_K=0. This verifies that every invocation of the induction hypothesis lowers the induction parameter.

source.place: Tag 051R proof, assertion dim(S\prime_K)<d, expanded by prime chains

proof.text: Apply the induction hypothesis to (R,C,N), or the zero-generic-algebra case, obtaining nonzero b in R for which N_b is free over R_b. Step 1 localizes the displayed short exact sequence; P_b=R_b[y_1,...,y_d] by sending each polynomial coefficient c/b^j to the corresponding fraction, with inverse obtained using a common denominator for its finitely many coefficients. Its monomials form an R_b-basis by the definition of a polynomial, so (P^{\oplus r})_b is free. Step 2 splits the localized sequence by lifts of the N_b-basis and supplies an R_b-basis of S_b. Undo the first localization as in step 4. This completes the domain case at dimension d.

For a general B and finite B-module M with dim(B_K)=d, B is Noetherian by finite-type permanence. Apply the prime-filtration theorem to obtain 0=M_0 contained in ... contained in M_n=M with M_i/M_{i-1} isomorphic to B/q_i for prime ideals q_i. Each S_i=B/q_i is a finite type domain algebra. If (S_i)_K is nonzero, its dimension is at most d: a chain of primes in (S_i)_K pulls back to a strict chain in B_K, as inverse image and quotient are inverse on ideals containing the kernel. Thus the domain case just proved at d, or the strong induction hypothesis below d, or the zero-generic-algebra case, gives a nonzero a_i in R for which (S_i)_{a_i} is free over R_{a_i}. Put a=\prod_i a_i (a=1 for the empty filtration); it is nonzero since R is a domain. Each a_i is a unit in R_a with inverse (\prod_{j\ne i}a_j)/a. Further localization preserves its basis by step 2. Localize the filtration using step 1; successively split each extension using step 2. The resulting union of the lifted quotient bases is an R_a-basis of M_a. This completes the strong induction and proves every clause of the item.
